The same caveats apply as for single equations: it does not always work. The crux of the difference: in Example 3.9.3, with f⃗ = [eᵗ; t] and e^t in the complementary solution, we do not know whether a⃗eᵗ conflicts with the complementary solution, so to be safe we try both a⃗eᵗ and b⃗teᵗ, x⃗ = a⃗eᵗ + b⃗teᵗ + c⃗t + d⃗, not just the term b⃗teᵗ; plugging in and identifying the coefficients of eᵗ, teᵗ, t and the constant vectors gives 8 equations, solved ad hoc, and both a⃗eᵗ and b⃗teᵗ really were needed. You can never go wrong by putting in more terms than needed; the extra coefficients turn out to be zero.

forms.condition: Example 3.9.3, f⃗(t) = [eᵗ; t] with eᵗ in the complementary solution

concepts.name: Variation of parameters for systems
concepts.statement: Variation of parameters works for any linear system x⃗′ = A(t)x⃗ + f⃗(t), equation (3.10), even if it is not constant-coefficient, provided we somehow solve the associated homogeneous problem and find a fundamental matrix solution X(t); for constant-coefficient systems it is essentially the integrating factor method. Try x⃗_p = X(t)u⃗(t) with u⃗(t) a vector-valued function instead of a constant. Substituting into (3.10), X′u⃗ + Xu⃗′ = AXu⃗ + f⃗, and since X′(t) = A(t)X(t) the X′u⃗ terms cancel, leaving X(t)u⃗′(t) = f⃗(t); so u⃗′ = [X(t)]⁻¹f⃗, integrate to get u⃗, and x⃗_p = X(t)∫[X(t)]⁻¹f⃗(t) dt. For a constant A with X(t) = e^(tA), [X(t)]⁻¹ = e^(−tA) and x⃗_p = e^(tA)∫e^(−tA)f⃗ dt, precisely the integrating factor result. Adding constants of integration adds X(t)c⃗, the complementary solution. In Example 3.9.4, X = [1 −t; t 1] gives x⃗_p = [t⁴/3; 2t³/3 + t].

forms.condition: X(t) a fundamental matrix solution of x⃗′ = A(t)x⃗

concepts.name: Undetermined coefficients for second-order systems
concepts.statement: For x⃗″ = Ax⃗ + F⃗(t) with A constant, the method is essentially the same as for first-order systems, with the simplifications of §3.6: if F⃗(t) = F⃗₀ cos(ωt), two derivatives of cosine is again cosine, so no sines are needed and the guess is x⃗_p = c⃗ cos(ωt). If F⃗ is a sum of cosines F⃗₀ cos(ω₀t) + F⃗₁ cos(ω₁t), by superposition try a⃗ cos(ω₀t) for the first problem and b⃗ cos(ω₁t) for the second and sum the solutions. If there is duplication with the complementary solution, or the equation has the form x⃗″ = Ax⃗′ + Bx⃗ + F⃗(t), do the same as for first-order systems.

concepts.name: Eigenvector decomposition for second-order systems
concepts.statement: For x⃗″ = Ax⃗ + f⃗(t) we can do eigenvector decomposition just like for first-order systems: with eigenvalues λ₁, …, λₙ, eigenvectors v⃗₁, …, v⃗ₙ and E = [v⃗₁ ⋯ v⃗ₙ], write x⃗(t) = v⃗₁ξ₁(t) + ⋯ + v⃗ₙξₙ(t) and f⃗(t) = v⃗₁g₁(t) + ⋯ + v⃗ₙgₙ(t) with g⃗ = E⁻¹f⃗. Plugging in and identifying coefficients as before gives the independent equations ξ_k″ = λ_kξ_k + g_k, each solved by the methods of Chapter 2; the general solutions for ξ₁ through ξₙ give the general solution x⃗. In Example 3.9.5, the forced two-cart system of §3.6 gives ξ₁″ = −ξ₁ + (2/3) cos(3t), ξ₂″ = −4ξ₂ − (2/3) cos(3t), C₁ = −1/12, C₂ = 2/15, and the particular solution [1/20; −3/10] cos(3t) as before.

concepts.name: Boundary value problem
concepts.statement: A boundary value problem, or endpoint problem, specifies the value of the solution (or its derivative) at two different points instead of the value and the derivative at a single point: for example x″ + λx = 0, x(a) = 0, x(b) = 0. As x = 0 is a solution, existence is not a problem; uniqueness is, and two conditions do not guarantee a unique solution.

concepts.name: Eigenvalue of a boundary value problem
concepts.statement: A number λ is an eigenvalue of (4.1), (4.2) or (4.3) if and only if there exists a nonzero (not identically zero) solution to the problem for that specific λ. This is the analogue of finding eigenvalues and eigenvectors of matrices; a differential operator has infinitely many eigenvalues.

forms.latex: x'' + \lambda x = 0, \quad x(a) = x(b), \quad x'(a) = x'(b)

concepts.name: Eigenfunction
concepts.statement: A nonzero solution of the boundary value problem for an eigenvalue λ is called a corresponding eigenfunction. Just like for eigenvectors, constant multiples of an eigenfunction are also eigenfunctions, so only one needs to be picked.

concepts.name: Eigenvalue problem of a differential operator
concepts.statement: Think of a function x(t) as a vector with infinitely many components, one for each t, and of L = −d²/dt² as a linear operator: the eigenvalue–eigenfunction pair is λ and a nonzero x with Lx = λx, that is, (L − λ)x = 0 under the endpoint conditions. A lot of the formalism of linear algebra still applies.

concepts.name: Finding eigenvalues and eigenfunctions
concepts.statement: Handle the cases λ > 0, λ = 0 and λ < 0 separately: write the general solution of x″ + λx = 0 in each case (A cos √λ t + B sin √λ t; At + B; A cosh √−λ t + B sinh √−λ t), impose the endpoint conditions, and keep the λ for which A and B need not both be zero; sinh ξ is zero only at ξ = 0, so there are no negative eigenvalues for these problems.

concepts.name: Eigenvalues with the solution zero at both ends
concepts.statement: For x″ + λx = 0, x(0) = 0, x(π) = 0, the eigenvalues are λ_k = k² with eigenfunctions x_k = sin(kt) for all integers k ≥ 1; λ = 0 is not an eigenvalue and there are no negative eigenvalues. On an interval of length L the eigenvalues are k²π²/L² with eigenfunctions sin(kπx/L).

forms.latex: \lambda_k = k^2 \qquad \text{with an eigenfunction} \qquad x_k = \sin (k t) \qquad \text{for all integers } k \geq 1
forms.ktex: \klambdak = k^2 \qquad \text{with an eigenfunction} \qquad \kxk = \sin (k t) \qquad \text{for all integers } k \geq 1

concepts.name: Eigenvalues with the derivative zero at both ends
concepts.statement: For x″ + λx = 0, x′(0) = 0, x′(π) = 0, the eigenvalues are λ_k = k² with eigenfunctions x_k = cos(kt) for k ≥ 1, and there is another eigenvalue λ₀ = 0 with the eigenfunction x₀ = 1; there are no negative eigenvalues.

concepts.name: Eigenvalues with periodic conditions
concepts.statement: For x″ + λx = 0, x(−π) = x(π), x′(−π) = x′(π), the eigenvalues are λ_k = k² for k ≥ 1, each with two linearly independent eigenfunctions cos(kt) and sin(kt), and λ₀ = 0 with the eigenfunction x₀ = 1; there are no negative eigenvalues. This is the problem that leads to the general Fourier series.

forms.latex: \lambda_k = k^2 \quad \text{with eigenfunctions} \quad \cos (k t) \text{ and } \sin (k t) \quad (k \geq 1), \qquad \lambda_0 = 0 \quad \text{with} \quad x_0 = 1
forms.ktex: \klambdak = k^2 \quad \text{with eigenfunctions} \quad \cos (k t) \text{ and } \sin (k t) \quad (k \geq 1), \qquad \klambdazero = 0 \quad \text{with} \quad x_0 = 1

concepts.name: Symmetric matrix
concepts.statement: A matrix is symmetric if A = Aᵀ, it is equal to its transpose. Eigenvectors for two distinct eigenvalues of a symmetric matrix are orthogonal, and the differential operators of this chapter act much like a symmetric matrix.

concepts.name: Orthogonality of eigenfunctions
concepts.statement: Theorem 4.1.1: if x₁(t) and x₂(t) are two eigenfunctions of (4.1), (4.2) or (4.3) for two different eigenvalues λ₁ and λ₂, then they are orthogonal in the sense that the integral of x₁(t)x₂(t) from a to b is 0. The integral is a type of inner product; for the trigonometric eigenfunctions this gives the integrals of sin(mt) sin(nt), cos(mt) cos(nt) and cos(mt) sin(nt) over [0, π] or [−π, π] that vanish for m ≠ n.

concepts.name: Fredholm alternative
concepts.statement: Theorem 4.1.2: exactly one of the following holds. Either x″ + λx = 0, x(a) = 0, x(b) = 0 has a nonzero solution, or x″ + λx = f(t), x(a) = 0, x(b) = 0 has a unique solution for every function f continuous on [a, b]. If λ is not an eigenvalue the nonhomogeneous problem has a unique solution for every right-hand side; if it is, the problem need not have a solution, and when it does the solution is not unique. The matrix version: either (A − λI)x⃗ = 0⃗ has a nontrivial solution or (A − λI)x⃗ = b⃗ has a unique solution for every b⃗.

concepts.name: Whirling string
concepts.statement: A tightly stretched string of linear density ρ and tension T, fixed at both ends of its length L and rotating at angular velocity ω, has deflection y(x) obeying Ty″ + ρω²y = 0, y(0) = 0, y(L) = 0. For most ω the string stays in the equilibrium y = 0; when ρω²/T = k²π²/L², that is ω = kπ√T/(L√ρ), it pops out some distance B in the shape of a sine wave crossing the x-axis k − 1 times. The amount B cannot be computed from this information.

concepts.name: Periodic function
concepts.statement: A function is periodic with period P if f(t) = f(t + P) for all t; for brevity f(t) is P-periodic. A P-periodic function is also 2P-periodic, 3P-periodic and so on; cos(kt) and sin(kt) are 2π-periodic for all integers k, and the constant functions are periodic for any period.

concepts.name: Periodic extension
concepts.statement: To extend a function f(t) defined on [−L, L] periodically is to define a 2L-periodic F(t) with F(t) = f(t) on [−L, L], F(t) = f(t − 2L) on [L, 3L], F(t) = f(t + 2L) on [−3L, −L], and so on; this needs f(−L) = f(L), or f defined on (−L, L] with f(−L) set to f(L). A formula for f(t) need not hold for its extension.

concepts.name: Decomposition along orthogonal vectors
concepts.statement: Eigenvectors of a symmetric matrix for distinct eigenvalues are orthogonal, ⟨v⃗, w⃗⟩ = v⃗ᵀw⃗ = 0. To write v⃗ = a₁w⃗₁ + a₂w⃗₂ in terms of mutually orthogonal w⃗₁ and w⃗₂, take the inner product with each: a₁ = ⟨v⃗, w⃗₁⟩/⟨w⃗₁, w⃗₁⟩ and a₂ = ⟨v⃗, w⃗₂⟩/⟨w⃗₂, w⃗₂⟩.

concepts.name: Fourier series
concepts.statement: The Fourier series, or trigonometric series, of a 2π-periodic function f(t) is its representation a₀/2 + Σ [a_n cos(nt) + b_n sin(nt)] in the eigenfunctions 1, cos(kt), sin(kt) of the periodic eigenvalue problem, the coefficient of 1 written as a₀/2 for convenience.

concepts.name: Harmonic
concepts.statement: The term a_n cos(nt) + b_n sin(nt) of a Fourier series is sometimes called the nth harmonic.

concepts.name: Inner product of functions
concepts.statement: The inner product of two functions on [−π, π] is ⟨f(t), g(t)⟩ = ∫ f(t)g(t) dt from −π to π. With it the eigenfunctions cos(kt) (the constant included) and sin(kt) are orthogonal, ⟨cos nt, cos nt⟩ = ⟨sin nt, sin nt⟩ = π for n ≥ 1, and ⟨1, 1⟩ = 2π.

concepts.name: Fourier coefficients
concepts.statement: The coefficients of the Fourier series are the projections of f(t) onto the eigenfunctions: a_n = ⟨f, cos nt⟩/⟨cos nt, cos nt⟩ = (1/π)∫ f(t) cos(nt) dt and b_n = (1/π)∫ f(t) sin(nt) dt over [−π, π], and a₀ = (1/π)∫ f(t) dt. They follow from the orthogonality of the eigenfunctions: taking the inner product of the series with cos(mt) leaves only a_m⟨cos mt, cos mt⟩.

forms.latex: a_n = \frac{1}{\pi} \int_{-\pi}^\pi f(t) \cos (nt) \, dt , \qquad b_n = \frac{1}{\pi} \int_{-\pi}^\pi f(t) \sin (nt) \, dt

concepts.name: Odd function
concepts.statement: An odd function is a function φ(t) with φ(−t) = −φ(t): t, sin t and t cos(nt) are odd.

concepts.name: Even function
concepts.statement: An even function is a function φ(t) with φ(−t) = φ(t): cos(nt) and t sin(nt) are even.

concepts.name: Integrals over a symmetric interval
concepts.statement: The integral of an odd function over a symmetric interval is zero, and the integral of an even function over a symmetric interval is twice the integral of the same function over half the interval; these facts from calculus do most of the work of computing Fourier coefficients.

concepts.name: Sawtooth
concepts.statement: The sawtooth is f(t) = t on (−π, π], extended periodically; it finds many applications, for example in electronic music. Its Fourier series is Σ 2(−1)^(n+1)/n · sin(nt), with a₀ = a_n = 0 because t and t cos(nt) are odd.

concepts.name: Square wave
concepts.statement: The square wave is f(t) = 0 on (−π, 0] and π on (0, π], extended periodically: the signal of a switch flipped on and off. Its Fourier series is π/2 + Σ over odd n of (2/n) sin(nt); at the discontinuities the series gives π/2, the midpoint, and redefining f there makes the equality hold everywhere.

concepts.name: Gibbs phenomenon
concepts.statement: Near a discontinuity the error of the partial sums, the overshoot, does not get smaller as more harmonics are taken; the region where the error is large does get smaller the more terms are taken.

concepts.name: Fundamental frequency
concepts.statement: A periodic signal is a superposition of pure frequencies; its base frequency, the musical note the sound is identified as, is the fundamental frequency, and for a vibrating string it is πa/L, which rises as the length L falls.

concepts.name: Overtones
concepts.statement: The higher frequencies of a signal, multiples of the fundamental frequency, are called the overtones in music; a pure sine wave has none, and a square wave has many, which is why it sounds so different from a pure tone.

concepts.name: Spectrum
concepts.statement: The set of all the frequencies that appear in a signal is called its spectrum.

concepts.name: Half period
concepts.statement: For a 2L-periodic function the number L is called the half period; the most common half periods in examples are π and 1.

concepts.name: Fourier series of a 2L-periodic function
concepts.statement: The Fourier series of a 2L-periodic f(t) is obtained by the change of variables s = πt/L, which makes g(s) = f(Ls/π) 2π-periodic: f(t) = a₀/2 + Σ [a_n cos(nπt/L) + b_n sin(nπt/L)] with a₀ = (1/L)∫ f dt, a_n = (1/L)∫ f cos(nπt/L) dt and b_n = (1/L)∫ f sin(nπt/L) dt over [−L, L]. No new mathematics: only different units for time.

forms.latex: a_0 = \frac{1}{L} \int_{-L}^L f(t) \, dt , \qquad a_n = \frac{1}{L} \int_{-L}^L f(t) \cos \left( \frac{n \pi}{L} t \right) dt , \qquad b_n = \frac{1}{L} \int_{-L}^L f(t) \sin \left( \frac{n \pi}{L} t \right) dt

concepts.name: One-sided limit
concepts.statement: f(c−) is the limit of f(t) as t approaches c from below (t < c) and f(c+) the limit as t approaches c from above (t > c); for the square wave f(0−) = 0 and f(0+) = π.

forms.latex: f(c-) = \lim_{t \uparrow c} f(t), \qquad f(c+) = \lim_{t \downarrow c} f(t)

concepts.name: Piecewise continuous function
concepts.statement: A function f(t) on [a, b] is piecewise continuous if there are finitely many points a = t₀ < t₁ < … < t_k = b such that f is continuous on each open interval (t_{i−1}, t_i) and all the one-sided limits f(t₀+), f(t₁−), f(t₁+), …, f(t_k−) exist and are finite.

concepts.name: Piecewise smooth function
concepts.statement: A piecewise continuous f(t) is piecewise smooth if moreover it is differentiable at all but finitely many points and f′(t) is piecewise continuous: the square wave and |t| are piecewise smooth; 1/t is not even piecewise continuous on [−1, 1], and the cube root of t is continuous but its derivative is unbounded near zero.

concepts.name: Convergence of a Fourier series
concepts.statement: Theorem 4.3.1: the Fourier series of a 2L-periodic piecewise smooth f(t) converges for all t. Where f is continuous it converges to f(t); otherwise it converges to the average (f(t−) + f(t+))/2 of the one-sided limits. Redefining f at each discontinuity to that average makes the series equal f everywhere; the theorem does not say how fast the series converges.

concepts.name: Differentiating a Fourier series term by term
concepts.statement: Theorem 4.3.2: if f(t) is a piecewise smooth continuous function with Fourier series a₀/2 + Σ [a_n cos(nπt/L) + b_n sin(nπt/L)] and f′(t) is piecewise smooth, then f′(t) = Σ [(−a_n nπ/L) sin(nπt/L) + (b_n nπ/L) cos(nπt/L)]. The function must be continuous: it can have corners but no jumps, or the differentiated series fails to converge.

concepts.name: Integrating a Fourier series term by term
concepts.statement: Theorem 4.3.3: if f(t) is piecewise smooth with Fourier series a₀/2 + Σ [a_n cos(nπt/L) + b_n sin(nπt/L)], its antiderivative is obtained term by term: F(t) = a₀t/2 + C + Σ [(a_n L/(nπ)) sin(nπt/L) − (b_n L/(nπ)) cos(nπt/L)], with F′ = f and C arbitrary. Because of the a₀t/2 term the result is not a Fourier series unless a₀ = 0: the antiderivative of a periodic function need not be periodic.

forms.latex: F(t) = \frac{a_0 t}{2} + C + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \Bigl[ \frac{a_n L}{n \pi} \sin \Bigl( \frac{n \pi}{L} t \Bigr) + \frac{-b_n L}{n \pi} \cos \Bigl( \frac{n \pi}{L} t \Bigr) \Bigr]
forms.ktex: \kF(t) = \frac{\kazero t}{2} + C + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \Bigl[ \frac{\kan L}{n \pi} \sin \Bigl( \frac{n \pi}{L} t \Bigr) + \frac{-\kbn L}{n \pi} \cos \Bigl( \frac{n \pi}{L} t \Bigr) \Bigr]

concepts.name: Decay of the coefficients and smoothness
concepts.statement: The more derivatives a function has, the faster its Fourier coefficients go to zero: with discontinuities they decay like 1/n, for a continuous function with corners like 1/n², for a function with one derivative but not two like 1/n³ (as for the piecewise parabola of Example 4.3.6, whose b_n = 8/(π³n³) for odd n). In reverse, coefficients decaying like 1/n² give a continuous function and like 1/n³ an everywhere differentiable one; differentiating Σ sin(nt)/n³ term by term reaches a sawtooth-like f″ and then a series that does not converge.

concepts.name: Odd periodic extension
concepts.statement: For f(t) defined on [0, L], F_odd(t) is f(t) for 0 ≤ t ≤ L and −f(−t) for −L < t < 0, extended to be 2L-periodic; it is odd, and one generally assumes f(0) = f(L) = 0.

concepts.name: Even periodic extension
concepts.statement: For f(t) defined on [0, L], F_even(t) is f(t) for 0 ≤ t ≤ L and f(−t) for −L < t < 0, extended to be 2L-periodic; it is even.

forms.latex: F_{\text{even}}(t) \overset{\text{def}}{=} \begin{cases} f(t) & \text{if } \; \phantom{-}0 \leq t \leq L , \\ f(-t) & \text{if } \; {-L} < t < 0 \end{cases}

concepts.name: Sine series
concepts.statement: The sine series of f(t) on [0, L] is the Fourier series of its odd periodic extension, Σ b_n sin(nπt/L) with b_n = (2/L)∫ f(t) sin(nπt/L) dt over [0, L]: an odd function has no cosine terms, and the coefficients are computed by integrating over the half-interval only.

concepts.name: Cosine series
concepts.statement: The cosine series of f(t) on [0, L] is the Fourier series of its even periodic extension, a₀/2 + Σ a_n cos(nπt/L) with a_n = (2/L)∫ f(t) cos(nπt/L) dt over [0, L], the formula holding for n = 0 as well: an even function has no sine terms.

concepts.name: Series of the odd and even extensions
concepts.statement: Theorem 4.4.1: for a piecewise smooth f(t) on [0, L], the odd periodic extension has the sine series with b_n = (2/L)∫₀ᴸ f(t) sin(nπt/L) dt and the even periodic extension has the cosine series with a_n = (2/L)∫₀ᴸ f(t) cos(nπt/L) dt. One usually does not care what happens outside [0, L] and picks whichever series fits the problem; the coefficients' decay tells whether the chosen extension has jumps (1/n) or only corners (1/n²).

concepts.name: Eigenfunction expansion
concepts.statement: The sine series is the expansion of f(t) in the eigenfunctions of x″ + λx = 0, x(0) = 0, x(L) = 0, and the cosine series the expansion in those of x′(0) = 0, x′(L) = 0; the same formulas come from the inner product ⟨f, g⟩ = ∫₀ᴸ f(t)g(t) dt and the procedure of 4.2. A question that leads to another eigenvalue problem still has an eigenfunction expansion, generalized in Chapter 5.

concepts.name: Dirichlet boundary conditions
concepts.statement: The conditions x(0) = 0, x(L) = 0 on the boundary value problem x″ + λx = f(t), 0 < t < L, are the Dirichlet boundary conditions; the eigenfunctions of the underlying problem are sin(nπt/L), so the problem is solved with sine series.

concepts.name: Neumann boundary conditions
concepts.statement: The conditions x′(0) = 0, x′(L) = 0 are the Neumann boundary conditions; the problem is solved the same way with cosine series.

concepts.name: Solving a boundary value problem by series
concepts.statement: To solve x″ + λx = f(t) with Dirichlet (or Neumann) conditions when λ is not an eigenvalue, write f(t) as a sine (or cosine) series with coefficients c_n, write x(t) as the same kind of series with unknown coefficients, substitute into the equation, and match coefficients: b_n(λ − n²π²/L²) = c_n. The eigenfunctions satisfy the boundary conditions, so x does too; that the factor is never zero is precisely the Fredholm alternative.

forms.condition: Example 4.4.3, x″ + 2x = t with x(0) = x(1) = 0

concepts.name: Periodically forced oscillation
concepts.statement: For the mass-spring system mx″ + cx′ + kx = F(t) with a 2L-periodic forcing F(t), the general solution is the complementary solution x_c, which decays when c > 0, plus a particular solution; the one of interest is the steady periodic solution x_sp, periodic with the same period as F(t). For c = 0 every solution is A cos(ω₀t) + B sin(ω₀t) + x_sp with ω₀ = √(k/m).

concepts.name: Steady periodic solution by Fourier series
concepts.statement: In the spirit of undetermined coefficients, write the forcing as F(t) = c₀/2 + Σ [c_n cos(nπt/L) + d_n sin(nπt/L)] and propose x(t) = a₀/2 + Σ [a_n cos(nπt/L) + b_n sin(nπt/L)] with unknown a_n and b_n; plug x into the equation and solve for a_n and b_n in terms of c_n and d_n, harmonic by harmonic. The result contains no terms of the complementary solution and has the period of F, so it is the steady periodic solution.

forms.latex: x_{sp}(t) = \frac{1}{4} + \sum_{\substack{n=1 \\ n \text{ odd}}}^\infty \frac{2}{\pi n (2 - n^2 \pi^2 )} \sin (n \pi t)
forms.condition: Example 4.5.1, x″ + 2x = F(t) with the jetpack's step forcing

concepts.name: Resonance with a periodic forcing
concepts.statement: With c = 0, if ω₀ = Nπ/L for some positive integer N, the Nth harmonic of F(t) coincides with the complementary solution and the usual guess gives a contradiction; the offending term is multiplied by t: x(t) = a₀/2 + t(a_N cos(Nπt/L) + b_N sin(Nπt/L)) + Σ over n ≠ N. The t-terms eventually dominate and lead to wild oscillations, pure resonance; the solution is no longer periodic. Any of the infinitely many overtones of F could hit ω₀ as the base frequency changes, though only the first few matter in practice. With c > 0 there is no pure resonance, only practical resonance, where one coefficient of x_sp gets very big.

forms.latex: x(t) = \frac{a_0}{2} + t \Biggl( a_N \cos \Bigl( \frac{N \pi}{L} t \Bigr) + b_N \sin \Bigl( \frac{N \pi}{L} t \Bigr) \Biggr) + \sum_{\substack{n=1\\n \neq N}}^\infty \Bigl[ a_n \cos \Bigl( \frac{n \pi}{L} t \Bigr) + b_n \sin \Bigl( \frac{n \pi}{L} t \Bigr) \Bigr]
forms.ktex: \kx(t) = \frac{\kazero}{2} + t \Biggl( a_N \cos \Bigl( \frac{N \pi}{L} t \Bigr) + b_N \sin \Bigl( \frac{N \pi}{L} t \Bigr) \Biggr) + \sum_{\substack{n=1\\n \neq N}}^\infty \Bigl[ \kan \cos \Bigl( \frac{n \pi}{L} t \Bigr) + \kbn \sin \Bigl( \frac{n \pi}{L} t \Bigr) \Bigr]

forms.latex: x_p(t) = \frac{-1}{9\pi^2} \, t \, \cos (3 \pi t) + \sum_{\substack{n=1 \\ n~\text{odd} \\ n \neq 3}}^\infty \frac{2}{\pi^3 n(9 - n^2)} \sin (n \pi t)
forms.ktex: \kxp(t) = \frac{-1}{9\pi^2} \, t \, \cos (3 \pi t) + \sum_{\substack{n=1 \\ n~\text{odd} \\ n \neq 3}}^\infty \frac{2}{\pi^3 n(9 - n^2)} \sin (n \pi t)
forms.condition: Example 4.5.2, 2x″ + 18π²x = F(t) with the ±1 square-wave forcing

concepts.name: Linear PDE
concepts.statement: A PDE is linear if the dependent variable and its derivatives appear at most to the first power and in no functions; only linear PDEs are treated.

concepts.name: Side conditions
concepts.statement: Together with a PDE one specifies boundary conditions, the value of the solution or its derivatives along the boundary of a region, and initial conditions, their values at some initial time; mixed together they are called side conditions. A side condition is homogeneous when u or a derivative of u is set to zero; the initial condition u(x, 0) = f(x) is not homogeneous.

concepts.name: Parabolic, hyperbolic and elliptic equations
concepts.statement: Three equations each represent a general class whose typical behavior it illustrates: the heat equation is a parabolic PDE, the wave equation a hyperbolic PDE and the Laplace equation an elliptic PDE.

concepts.name: Heat equation
concepts.statement: For a wire of length L insulated along its length, with u(x, t) the temperature at the point x at time t, the one-dimensional heat equation is ∂u/∂t = k ∂²u/∂x², or u_t = k u_xx in subscript notation, with k > 0 the thermal diffusivity: the change of heat in time at a point is proportional to the second x-derivative, so heat flows away from a maximum (concave down, u_t < 0) and into a minimum. It is solved on the region 0 < x < L, t > 0.

concepts.name: Thermal diffusivity
concepts.statement: The constant k > 0 of the heat equation u_t = k u_xx is the thermal diffusivity of the material.

concepts.name: Side conditions for the heat equation
concepts.statement: The ends of the wire are either kept at temperature 0, u(0, t) = 0 and u(L, t) = 0 for t > 0, or insulated, u_x(0, t) = 0 and u_x(L, t) = 0: where u_x is zero heat flows in neither direction, so u_x = 0 at an end means no heat flows in or out there. Two conditions go along the x-axis as there are two x-derivatives; both kinds are homogeneous. The initial condition is the temperature distribution u(x, 0) = f(x) for 0 < x < L.

concepts.name: Superposition for linear homogeneous PDEs
concepts.statement: The heat equation is linear and homogeneous, so the principle of superposition applies: if u₁ and u₂ are solutions and c₁, c₂ constants, then u = c₁u₁ + c₂u₂ is a solution. Superposition preserves all homogeneous side conditions: if u₁ and u₂ satisfy u(0, t) = u(L, t) = 0, or u_x(0, t) = u_x(L, t) = 0, so does c₁u₁ + c₂u₂.

concepts.name: Separation of variables
concepts.statement: The method of separation of variables looks for solutions that are products of functions of one variable, u(x, t) = X(x)T(t): enough building-block solutions of this form satisfying the equation and the homogeneous side conditions are found, and the desired solution to the nonhomogeneous initial condition is built from them by superposition.

concepts.name: The heat equation separated
concepts.statement: Plugging u = X(x)T(t) into u_t = k u_xx gives X(x)T′(t) = kX″(x)T(t), so T′/(kT) = X″/X; one side does not depend on x and the other not on t, so both equal a constant, called −λ for convenience: X″ + λX = 0 and T′ + λkT = 0. The side conditions u(0, t) = u(L, t) = 0 give X(0) = X(L) = 0, an eigenvalue problem with λ_n = n²π²/L² and X_n = sin(nπx/L); then T_n = e^(−n²π²kt/L²), one of the fundamental equations, chosen with T_n(0) = 1, and u_n = X_nT_n are the building blocks.

forms.latex: u_n(x,t) = X_n(x)T_n(t) = \sin \left( \frac{n \pi}{L} x \right) e^{\frac{-n^2 \pi^2}{L^2} k t}

concepts.name: Solution of the heat equation with the ends at zero
concepts.statement: With u(0, t) = u(L, t) = 0 and u(x, 0) = f(x), write f as the sine series Σ b_n sin(nπx/L), the Fourier series of its odd periodic extension; then u(x, t) = Σ b_n sin(nπx/L) e^(−n²π²kt/L²). It solves the equation by superposition, the sines vanish at the ends, and at t = 0 every T_n is 1 so the series is f(x). For large t only the first one or two terms matter, since the others decay much faster.

forms.latex: u(x,t) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty b_n u_n(x,t) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty b_n \sin \left( \frac{n \pi}{L} x \right) e^{\frac{-n^2 \pi^2}{L^2} k t}

concepts.name: Solution of the heat equation with insulated ends
concepts.statement: With u_x(0, t) = u_x(L, t) = 0 the eigenfunctions are X_n = cos(nπx/L) for n ≥ 0 (X₀ = 1 with T₀ = 1), so write f as the cosine series a₀/2 + Σ a_n cos(nπx/L), the Fourier series of its even periodic extension, and u(x, t) = a₀/2 + Σ a_n cos(nπx/L) e^(−n²π²kt/L²). As time goes on every term but the constant dies out and the temperature evens out across the wire.

forms.latex: u(x,t) = \frac{a_0}{2} + \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n u_n(x,t) = \frac{a_0}{2} + \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n \cos \left( \frac{n \pi}{L} x \right) e^{\frac{-n^2 \pi^2}{L^2} k t}

concepts.name: Smoothing by the heat equation
concepts.statement: The heat equation smooths out f(x) as t grows: for fixed t > 0 the solution is a Fourier series with coefficients b_n e^(−n²π²kt/L²), which go to zero faster than any 1/nᵖ, so u(x, t) as a function of x has infinitely many derivatives even if f has jumps and corners.

concepts.name: Average temperature of an insulated wire
concepts.statement: The constant term a₀/2 = (1/L)∫₀ᴸ f(x) dx is the average value of f(x), the average of the initial temperature. As the wire is insulated everywhere no heat gets in or out, so the average temperature is always a₀/2, and as t → ∞ the temperature goes to the constant a₀/2 everywhere.

concepts.name: Wave equation
concepts.statement: For a tensioned string of length L vibrating in one direction, with y(x, t) the displacement from rest at the position x and time t, the one-dimensional wave equation is y_tt = a²y_xx for a constant a > 0: the acceleration at a point is proportional to the second derivative of the shape, so where the string is concave down it accelerates downward. It is a hyperbolic PDE, solved on 0 < x < L, t > 0.

concepts.name: Side conditions for the wave equation
concepts.statement: The ends are fixed, y(0, t) = 0 and y(L, t) = 0 for t > 0; and since there are two t-derivatives two further conditions are needed, the initial position y(x, 0) = f(x) and the initial velocity y_t(x, 0) = g(x) for 0 < x < L.

forms.latex: \begin{array}{ll} y_{tt} = a^2 y_{xx} & \text{for } 0 < x < L \text{ and } t > 0, \\ y(0,t) = y(L,t) = 0 & \text{for } t > 0, \\ y(x,0) = f(x) & \text{for } 0 < x < L , \\ y_t(x,0) = g(x) & \text{for } 0 < x < L \end{array}
forms.ktex: \begin{array}{ll} \kytt = a^2 \kyxx & \text{for } 0 < x < L \text{ and } t > 0, \\ \ky(0,t) = \ky(L,t) = 0 & \text{for } t > 0, \\ \ky(x,0) = \kf(x) & \text{for } 0 < x < L , \\ \kyt(x,0) = \kg(x) & \text{for } 0 < x < L \end{array}

concepts.name: Splitting the wave problem in two
concepts.statement: Superposition only works for homogeneous conditions, so the problem is split: w solves (4.11) with w(x, 0) = 0 and w_t(x, 0) = g(x), z solves (4.12) with z(x, 0) = f(x) and z_t(x, 0) = 0, and y = w + z solves the wave equation with both nonhomogeneous initial conditions. Each half has only one nonhomogeneous condition, so separation of variables finds its building blocks.

forms.latex: w_{tt} = a^2 w_{xx}, \quad w(0,t) = w(L,t) = 0, \quad w(x,0) = 0, \quad w_t(x,0) = g(x)
z_{tt} = a^2 z_{xx}, \quad z(0,t) = z(L,t) = 0, \quad z(x,0) = f(x), \quad z_t(x,0) = 0

concepts.name: Series solution of the wave equation
concepts.statement: Theorem 4.7.1: for the problem (4.14) with f(x) = Σ c_n sin(nπx/L) and g(x) = Σ b_n sin(nπx/L), the solution is y(x, t) = Σ sin(nπx/L) [b_n (L/(nπa)) sin(nπat/L) + c_n cos(nπat/L)], the sum of the building blocks w_n = (L/(nπa)) sin(nπx/L) sin(nπat/L) of (4.11) and z_n = sin(nπx/L) cos(nπat/L) of (4.12). Separation gives X″ + λX = 0 and T″ + λa²T = 0; the T's are sines and cosines, and the shape does not get smoother in time: the sharp edges remain.

forms.latex: y(x,t) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \sin \left( \frac{n \pi}{L} x \right) \left[ b_n \frac{L}{n \pi a} \sin \left( \frac{n \pi a}{L} t \right) + c_n \cos \left( \frac{n \pi a}{L} t \right) \right]
forms.ktex: \ky(x,t) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \sin \left( \frac{n \pi}{L} x \right) \left[ \kbn \frac{L}{n \pi a} \sin \left( \frac{n \pi a}{L} t \right) + \kcn \cos \left( \frac{n \pi a}{L} t \right) \right]

forms.latex: w_n(x,t) = \frac{L}{n \pi a} \sin \left( \frac{n \pi}{L} x \right) \sin \left( \frac{n \pi a}{L} t \right), \qquad z_n(x,t) = \sin \left( \frac{n \pi}{L} x \right) \cos \left( \frac{n \pi a}{L} t \right)
forms.ktex: \kwn(x,t) = \frac{L}{n \pi a} \sin \left( \frac{n \pi}{L} x \right) \sin \left( \frac{n \pi a}{L} t \right), \qquad \kzn(x,t) = \sin \left( \frac{n \pi}{L} x \right) \cos \left( \frac{n \pi a}{L} t \right)

concepts.name: Timbre
concepts.statement: The angular frequencies of a vibrating string are nπa/L: the fundamental frequency πa/L and all its multiples, the overtones. Which overtones appear and with what amplitude is what musicians call the timbre of the note and mathematicians the spectrum; because every frequency is a multiple of one, the sound is pleasing. A sharper pluck, or one closer to the bridge, has coefficients that decay more slowly and a sound with more high overtones.

concepts.name: Wave speed and the string's tension
concepts.statement: The constant a is √(T/ρ), with T the tension and ρ the linear density of the string: tightening the string raises a and the fundamental frequency πa/L, a heavier string lowers them, and a shorter string (a finger on the fingerboard) raises the note.

concepts.name: Symmetry between space and time
concepts.statement: Except for the constant a, the solution sin(nπx/L) sin(nπat/L) looks the same with time and space flipped: for a fixed x the solution is a Fourier series in t, for a fixed t a Fourier series in x, with related coefficients, so corners in f(x) or g(x) become corners in the sound wave. In theory any timbre can be obtained by plucking the string the right way.

concepts.name: General solution of the wave equation
concepts.statement: In the characteristic coordinates ξ = x − at, η = x + at the chain rule gives ∂/∂x = ∂/∂ξ + ∂/∂η and ∂/∂t = −a∂/∂ξ + a∂/∂η, so a²y_xx − y_tt = 4a²y_ξη and the wave equation becomes y_ξη = 0. Integrating twice, once in each variable with a constant depending on the other, every solution is y = A(ξ) + B(η) = A(x − at) + B(x + at): a superposition of two waves traveling at speed a in opposite directions along the curves where ξ and η are constant. This is why the solution never gets nicer: corners in the initial conditions stay corners.

concepts.name: D'Alembert's formula
terms: d’Alembert solution to the wave equation
concepts.statement: With F(x) the odd periodic extension of f(x) and G(x) that of g(x), take A(x) = F(x)/2 − (1/2a)∫₀ˣ G(s) ds and B(x) = F(x)/2 + (1/2a)∫₀ˣ G(s) ds: the d'Alembert solution is y(x, t) = (F(x − at) + F(x + at))/2 + (1/2a)∫ G(s) ds from x − at to x + at. It gives y(x, 0) = F(x) and y_t(x, 0) = G(x) by the fundamental theorem of calculus, and y(0, t) = y(L, t) = 0 because F and G are odd and 2L-periodic. With H(x) = ∫₀ˣ G(s) ds it reads y = (F(x − at) + F(x + at))/2 + (−H(x − at) + H(x + at))/(2a): mind the minus sign and the a. It is much easier to compute and plot than the Fourier series; the odd periodic extensions must be used, since the formulas for f and g hold only on 0 < x < L.

forms.latex: A(x) = \frac{1}{2} F(x) - \frac{1}{2a} \int_0^x G(s) \,ds , \qquad B(x) = \frac{1}{2} F(x) + \frac{1}{2a} \int_0^x G(s) \,ds
y(x,t) = \frac{ F(x-at) + F(x+at) }{2} + \frac{ -H(x-at) + H(x+at) }{2a}, \qquad H(x) = \int_0^x G(s) \,ds

concepts.name: Wavefronts
concepts.statement: The solution at (x, t) uses the initial conditions only on the interval [x − at, x + at]; its endpoints are the wavefronts, where the wave front from a disturbance at x stands at time t. An observer at x = 0 at time t = 1 with a = 1 has seen only the initial conditions for x in [−1, 1] and is unaware of anything else, which is why a supernova is unknown until its light arrives.

concepts.name: Steady-state temperature
concepts.statement: The steady-state temperature distribution is the temperature after a long enough period of time: a solution of the heat equation that does not depend on time, u_t = 0. In one space variable it satisfies u_xx = 0, so u = Ax + B, and a wire with its ends held at T₁ and T₂ settles on the straight line u(x) = (T₂ − T₁)x/L + T₁.

concepts.name: Heat equation in two space variables
concepts.statement: In two space dimensions the heat equation is u_t = k(u_xx + u_yy), more commonly written u_t = kΔu or u_t = k∇²u; defining Δ for any number of space dimensions makes the heat equation always u_t = kΔu.

concepts.name: Laplacian
concepts.statement: The operator Δ, also written ∇², is ∂²/∂x² + ∂²/∂y², called the Laplacian.

forms.latex: \Delta u = \nabla^2 u = \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} + \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y^2}

concepts.name: Laplace equation
concepts.statement: A steady-state solution of the two-dimensional heat equation, u_t = 0, is a function u(x, y) with Δu = u_xx + u_yy = 0, the Laplace equation, an example of an elliptic equation.

concepts.name: Harmonic function
concepts.statement: Solutions of the Laplace equation are called harmonic functions, with many properties and applications beyond steady-state heat. In two variables they are no longer just linear (x² − y² and xy are harmonic), but where u_xx > 0 one has u_yy < 0, so a harmonic function can never have a hilltop or a valley: the hottest or coldest spot is not inside. A rubber sheet stretched over the region and fixed to a wire bent to the boundary temperatures approximates its graph.

concepts.name: Dirichlet problem
concepts.statement: A Dirichlet problem is the Laplace equation on a region of the xy-plane together with values specified along the boundary of the region; the solution u is harmonic on the region and agrees with the specified values on the boundary.

concepts.name: Dirichlet problem on a rectangle
concepts.statement: On the rectangle 0 < x < w, 0 < y < h with Δu = 0, u = 0 on the left, top and right edges and u(x, 0) = f(x) on the bottom, separation u = X(x)Y(y) gives X″ + λX = 0 and Y″ − λY = 0 with X(0) = X(w) = 0 and Y(h) = 0, so λ_n = n²π²/w², X_n = sin(nπx/w) and, choosing Y_n(0) = 1 and using sinh(α − β) = sinh α cosh β − cosh α sinh β, Y_n = sinh(nπ(h − y)/w)/sinh(nπh/w). With f(x) = Σ b_n sin(nπx/w) the solution is u(x, y) = Σ b_n sin(nπx/w) sinh(nπ(h − y)/w)/sinh(nπh/w). For Example 4.9.1, w = h = π and f = π, u = Σ over odd n of (4/n) sin(nx) sinh(n(π − y))/sinh(nπ).

forms.latex: u(x,y) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty b_n u_n(x,y) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty b_n \sin \left( \frac{n \pi}{w} x \right) \left( \frac{\sinh \left( \frac{n \pi (h-y) }{w} \right)} {\sinh \left( \frac{n \pi h }{w} \right)} \right)
\Delta u = 0, \quad u(0,y) = 0, \quad u(x,h) = 0, \quad u(w,y) = 0, \quad u(x,0) = f(x)
Y_n(y) = A_n \cosh \left( \frac{n \pi}{w} y \right) + B_n \sinh \left( \frac{n \pi}{w} y \right) = \frac{\sinh \left( \frac{n \pi (h-y) }{w} \right)} {\sinh \left( \frac{n \pi h }{w} \right)}

concepts.name: Superposing the four edge problems
concepts.statement: With arbitrary data on all four sides of the rectangle, solve four problems, each with one piece of nonhomogeneous data and zero on the other three edges, and add the four solutions by the principle of superposition.

concepts.name: Polar coordinates
concepts.statement: The polar coordinates of the (x, y)-plane are (r, θ) with x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ, r ≥ 0 and −π < θ ≤ π: the point (x, y) is at distance r from the origin at an angle θ from the positive x-axis. The circle is the natural setting for the Laplace equation, and polar coordinates are what makes it harder.

concepts.name: Laplacian in polar coordinates
concepts.statement: Computing u_r, u_rr, u_θ and u_θθ by the chain rule in terms of the x and y derivatives (with the product rule for the second derivatives), adding u_rr to u_θθ/r² and using cos²θ + sin²θ = 1 leaves u_xx + u_yy short of the term u_r/r: Δu = u_xx + u_yy = u_θθ/r² + u_r/r + u_rr. In polar coordinates the Laplacian no longer has constant coefficients.

forms.latex: \Delta u = u_{xx} + u_{yy} = \frac{1}{r^2} u_{\theta\theta} + \frac{1}{r} u_{r} + u_{rr}

concepts.name: Dirichlet problem on the disc
concepts.statement: For Δu = 0 on r < 1 with u(1, θ) = g(θ), separate u = R(r)Θ(θ): Θ″ + λΘ = 0 and r²R″ + rR′ − λR = 0. Since u must be 2π-periodic in θ, λ = n² for n = 0, 1, 2, … as in Example 4.1.5, with Θ₀ = a₀/2 and Θ_n = a_n cos(nθ) + b_n sin(nθ); the R equation (the one of Exercises 2.1.6–2.1.7) gives R₀ = A + B ln r and R_n = Arⁿ + Br⁻ⁿ, and finiteness at the origin forces B = 0, so R₀ = 1 and R_n = rⁿ. The solution is u(r, θ) = a₀/2 + Σ [a_n rⁿ cos(nθ) + b_n rⁿ sin(nθ)]: expand g(θ) as a Fourier series and multiply the nth term by rⁿ, with a_n = (1/π)∫ g(θ) cos(nθ) dθ and b_n = (1/π)∫ g(θ) sin(nθ) dθ over [−π, π]. A high frequency in g is felt mostly near the boundary, since rⁿ is small for r near 0.

forms.latex: a_n = \frac{1}{\pi} \int_{-\pi}^\pi g(\theta) \cos (n\theta) \, d\theta \qquad \text{and} \qquad b_n = \frac{1}{\pi} \int_{-\pi}^\pi g(\theta) \sin (n\theta) \, d\theta

concepts.name: Sum of a geometric series
concepts.statement: For a complex number z with |z| < 1, Σ zⁿ from n = 1 is z/(1 − z): the standard geometric series multiplied by z, since the sum starts at 1.

concepts.name: Poisson kernel
concepts.statement: The Poisson kernel is the function P(r, θ, α) with u(r, θ) = (1/2π)∫ P(r, θ, α) g(α) dα over [−π, π]: replacing the coefficients of the series solution by their integrals and writing everything as one integral gives P = 1 + 2Σ rⁿ cos(n(θ − α)), and complex exponentials with the geometric series sum it to P = (1 − r²)/(1 − 2r cos(θ − α) + r²), that is (1 − r²)/s² with s the distance from (r, θ) to (1, α). The integral is one to evaluate numerically, and since P has infinitely many derivatives so does u inside the circle. The same idea gives integral kernels for other equations with series solutions.

concepts.name: Average value of a harmonic function
concepts.statement: At the origin the Poisson formula gives u(0, 0) = (1/2π)∫ g(α) dα, the average value of g and so of u on the boundary; in general the value of a harmonic function at a point p equals the average of its values on a circle centered at p. At other points the formula is a weighted average of the boundary data: the kernel is bigger when (1, α) is closer to (r, θ), so nearby boundary values get more weight.

concepts.name: Robin boundary conditions
concepts.statement: Robin boundary conditions are the endpoint conditions hX(0) − X′(0) = 0 and hX(L) + X′(L) = 0 for some constant h; they come up when the ends of the wire are immersed in some medium.

concepts.name: Mixed boundary conditions
concepts.statement: Mixed boundary conditions set the value of X at one end and of its derivative at the other, X′(0) = 0 and X(L) = 0, or X(0) = 0 and X′(L) = 0.

concepts.name: Sturm–Liouville equation
concepts.statement: The second-order linear equation (p(x)y′)′ − q(x)y + λr(x)y = 0, equation (5.1); essentially any equation a(x)y″ + b(x)y′ + c(x)y + λd(x)y = 0 can be written in this form after multiplying by a proper factor.

concepts.name: Putting an equation into Sturm–Liouville form
concepts.statement: To write a(x)y″ + b(x)y′ + c(x)y + λd(x)y = 0 as (5.1), multiply by the factor that makes the first two terms a derivative of a product: Bessel's equation x²y″ + xy′ + (λx² − n²)y = 0 multiplied by 1/x becomes (xy′)′ − (n²/x)y + λxy = 0.

concepts.name: Sturm–Liouville problem
concepts.statement: The Sturm–Liouville problem is to seek nontrivial solutions y of (p(x)y′)′ − q(x)y + λr(x)y = 0 on a < x < b with α₁y(a) − α₂y′(a) = 0 and β₁y(b) + β₂y′(b) = 0, where α₁, α₂ are not both zero and neither are β₁, β₂; the λs that admit a nontrivial solution are the eigenvalues and the solutions are the eigenfunctions.

forms.latex: \begin{aligned} &\frac{d}{dx} \left( p(x) \frac{dy}{dx} \right) - q(x) y + \lambda r(x) y = 0, \qquad a < x < b, \\ &\alpha_1 y(a) - \alpha_2 y'(a) = 0, \\ &\beta_1 y(b) + \beta_2 y'(b) = 0. \end{aligned}

concepts.name: Regular Sturm–Liouville problem
concepts.statement: A regular Sturm–Liouville problem is one where p(x), p′(x), q(x) and r(x) are continuous on [a, b], p(x) > 0 and r(x) > 0 for all x in [a, b] including the endpoints, q(x) ≥ 0, and α₁, α₂, β₁, β₂ ≥ 0 with neither α₁ = α₂ = 0 nor β₁ = β₂ = 0.

concepts.name: Eigenvalues of a regular Sturm–Liouville problem
concepts.statement: If p, p′, q and r are continuous on [a, b] with p > 0 and r > 0 there, the Sturm–Liouville problem has an increasing sequence of eigenvalues λ₁ < λ₂ < λ₃ < ⋯ with λₙ → ∞, and to each λₙ there is, up to a constant multiple, a single eigenfunction yₙ(x). Moreover, if q ≥ 0 and α₁, α₂, β₁, β₂ ≥ 0, then λₙ ≥ 0 for all n (Theorem 5.1.1).

concepts.name: Finding eigenvalues from a transcendental equation
concepts.statement: When the boundary conditions lead to an equation such as h/√λ = tan √λ, the eigenvalues are found with a computer by plotting both sides, here h/x and tan x, and reading off the intersections √λ₁, √λ₂, …; for h = 1 the first two are 0.86 and 3.43, so λ₁ ≈ 0.74 and λ₂ ≈ 11.73, with eigenfunctions yₙ(x) = cos(√λₙ x) + (h/√λₙ) sin(√λₙ x) (Example 5.1.3).

concepts.name: Weight function
concepts.statement: A weight function r(x) on [a, b] is any function, generally assumed positive, that weights the integral of a product of two functions: those x where r(x) is greater have more weight. Nonconstant weights arise naturally from a change of variables, as if dξ = r(x) dx.

concepts.name: Orthogonality with respect to a weight
concepts.statement: Two functions f(x) and g(x) are orthogonal with respect to the weight function r(x) on [a, b] when ∫ₐᵇ f(x)g(x)r(x) dx = 0.

concepts.name: Inner product with respect to a weight
concepts.statement: The inner product of f and g with respect to the weight r is ⟨f, g⟩ = ∫ₐᵇ f(x)g(x)r(x) dx, and f and g are orthogonal whenever ⟨f, g⟩ = 0; the results and concepts are analogous to finite-dimensional linear algebra.

concepts.name: Orthogonality of Sturm–Liouville eigenfunctions
concepts.statement: For a regular Sturm–Liouville problem, two eigenfunctions y_j and y_k for two distinct eigenvalues λ_j and λ_k satisfy ∫ₐᵇ y_j(x)y_k(x)r(x) dx = 0: they are orthogonal with respect to the weight function r (Theorem 5.1.2).

concepts.name: Fredholm alternative for Sturm–Liouville problems
concepts.statement: For a regular Sturm–Liouville problem, either the homogeneous problem (p y′)′ − q y + λ r y = 0 with its endpoint conditions has a nonzero solution (λ is an eigenvalue), or the nonhomogeneous problem (p y′)′ − q y + λ r y = f(x) with the same conditions has a unique solution for any f continuous on [a, b] (Theorem 5.1.3). It says when a unique solution exists; to find it, f and y are decomposed in eigenfunctions of the homogeneous problem.

forms.latex: \frac{d}{dx} \left( p(x) \frac{dy}{dx} \right) - q(x) y + \lambda r(x) y = 0, \quad \alpha_1 y(a) - \alpha_2 y'(a) = 0, \quad \beta_1 y(b) + \beta_2 y'(b) = 0
\frac{d}{dx} \left( p(x) \frac{dy}{dx} \right) - q(x) y + \lambda r(x) y = f(x), \quad \alpha_1 y(a) - \alpha_2 y'(a) = 0, \quad \beta_1 y(b) + \beta_2 y'(b) = 0

concepts.name: Eigenfunction decomposition
concepts.statement: The eigenfunction decomposition of a function f(x) writes it as f(x) = Σ cₙyₙ(x), equation (5.3), where yₙ are the eigenfunctions of a Sturm–Liouville problem; the sine series is the case of y″ + λy = 0 with y(0) = y(L) = 0.

concepts.name: Coefficients of an eigenfunction series
concepts.statement: Assuming convergence and term-by-term integration, orthogonality gives ⟨f, yₘ⟩ = cₘ⟨yₘ, yₘ⟩, so the coefficients of (5.3) are cₘ = ⟨f, yₘ⟩/⟨yₘ, yₘ⟩ = ∫ₐᵇ f yₘ r dx / ∫ₐᵇ yₘ² r dx, equation (5.4); if each eigenfunction is scaled so that ⟨yₘ, yₘ⟩ = 1, simply cₘ = ⟨f, yₘ⟩.

forms.latex: c_m = \frac{\langle f , y_m \rangle}{\langle y_m , y_m \rangle} = \frac{\int_a^b f(x) \, y_m (x)\, r(x) \, dx} {\int_a^b {\bigl(y_m(x)\bigr)}^2 \, r(x) \,dx}

concepts.name: Convergence of an eigenfunction series
concepts.statement: If f is piecewise smooth and continuous on [a, b] and y₁, y₂, … are eigenfunctions of a regular Sturm–Liouville problem, one for each eigenvalue, then the constants c₁, c₂, … given by (5.4) make the series (5.3) converge and equal f(x) for a < x < b (Theorem 5.1.4).

concepts.name: Transversal vibrations
concepts.statement: Transversal vibrations of an elastic beam are the vibrations where the beam bends: with the beam along the x-axis, y(x, t) measures the displacement of the point x at time t.

concepts.name: Beam equation
concepts.statement: The transversal vibrations of a beam are governed by a⁴ ∂⁴y/∂x⁴ + ∂²y/∂t² = 0 for a constant a > 0 (a⁴ = EI/ρ). For a beam of length 1 simply supported at the ends, displaced to f(x) and let go from rest, y satisfies (5.5): y = y_xx = 0 at x = 0 and x = 1, y(x, 0) = f(x), y_t(x, 0) = 0.

forms.latex: \begin{aligned} & a^4 y_{xxxx} + y_{tt} = 0 \qquad (0 < x < 1, \enspace t > 0), \\ & y(0,t) = y_{xx}(0,t) = 0 , \\ & y(1,t) = y_{xx}(1,t) = 0 , \\ & y(x,0) = f(x), \qquad y_{t}(x,0) = 0 . \end{aligned}
forms.condition: length 1, hinged ends, released from rest

concepts.name: Fourth-order eigenvalue problem
concepts.statement: Separating y(x, t) = X(x)T(t) in the beam equation gives X⁽⁴⁾/X = −T″/(a⁴T) = λ, so T″ + λa⁴T = 0 and X⁽⁴⁾ − λX = 0 with X(0) = X″(0) = 0 and X(1) = X″(1) = 0; it is not a Sturm–Liouville problem, but the idea is the same, and physical intuition (vibration, not growth or decay) says λ > 0.

concepts.name: Series solution of the hinged beam
concepts.statement: With ω = ⁴√λ, the general solution Ae^(ωx) + Be^(−ωx) + C sin(ωx) + D cos(ωx) of X⁽⁴⁾ − ω⁴X = 0 meets the hinged conditions only for ω = nπ, so the eigenvalues are λₙ = n⁴π⁴ with eigenfunctions sin(nπx), the time factors are Tₙ(t) = cos(n²π²a²t), and with f(x) = Σ bₙ sin(nπx) the solution of (5.5) is y(x, t) = Σ bₙ sin(nπx) cos(n²π²a²t).

forms.latex: y(x,t) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty b_n X_n(x) T_n(t) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty b_n \sin (n \pi x) \cos ( n^2 \pi^2 a^2 t )

concepts.name: Natural frequencies of a hinged beam
concepts.statement: The natural angular frequencies of the simply supported beam are n²π²a², all integer multiples of the fundamental π²a², but only the square multiples 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, …, where a vibrating string gives all of 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, …; the beam's timbre is therefore much closer to a pure sound, the xylophone or vibraphone against the guitar or piano.

concepts.name: Hinged end
concepts.statement: At a hinged (simply supported) end of a beam, say x = 0, the displacement and its second derivative vanish: y(0, t) = y_xx(0, t) = 0.

concepts.name: Free end
concepts.statement: At a free end of a beam, one just floating in air, the second and third derivatives vanish: y_xx(0, t) = y_xxx(0, t) = 0.

concepts.name: Clamped end
concepts.statement: At a clamped or fixed end of a beam, for example one welded to a wall, the displacement and the slope vanish: y(0, t) = y_x(0, t) = 0.

concepts.name: Natural frequencies of a string
concepts.statement: The natural (angular) frequencies of the string of length L with fixed ends are nπa/L for integers n ≥ 1, the frequencies of the free vibrations y = Σ (Aₙ cos(nπat/L) + Bₙ sin(nπat/L)) sin(nπx/L); the base frequency is πa/L.

forms.latex: y = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \left( A_n \cos \left( \frac{n\pi a}{L} t \right) + B_n \sin \left( \frac{n\pi a}{L} t \right) \right) \sin \left( \frac{n\pi}{L} x \right)

concepts.name: Forced wave equation
concepts.statement: With an external force uniform along the string, F₀ cos(ωt) as force per unit mass (the forcing function), the wave equation becomes y_tt = a²y_xx + F₀ cos(ωt), equation (5.7), with the same boundary conditions; the string initially at rest satisfies (5.8): y(0, t) = y(L, t) = 0, y(x, 0) = 0, y_t(x, 0) = 0.

concepts.name: Solving the forced string as y = y_c + y_p
concepts.statement: First find a particular solution y_p of (5.7) satisfying only y(0, t) = y(L, t) = 0; then define f(x) = −y_p(x, 0) and g(x) = −∂y_p/∂t(x, 0) and find the solution y_c of the free problem (5.6) with these initial conditions; then y = y_c + y_p solves (5.7) with the initial conditions (5.8).

forms.latex: f(x) = -y_p(x,0), \qquad g(x) = -\frac{\partial y_p}{\partial t} (x,0), \qquad y = y_c + y_p

concepts.name: Particular solution of the forced string
concepts.statement: The guess y_p = X(x) cos(ωt) in (5.7) gives −ω²X = a²X″ + F₀, whose general solution is X = A cos(ωx/a) + B sin(ωx/a) − F₀/ω²; X(0) = 0 gives A = F₀/ω², and X(L) = 0 gives B = −F₀(cos(ωL/a) − 1)/(ω² sin(ωL/a)), equation (5.9), when sin(ωL/a) ≠ 0; so y_p(x, t) = (F₀/ω²)(cos(ωx/a) − ((cos(ωL/a) − 1)/sin(ωL/a)) sin(ωx/a) − 1) cos(ωt).

forms.latex: y_p(x,t) = \frac{F_0}{\omega^2} \left( \cos \left( \frac{\omega}{a} x \right) - \frac{\cos \left( \frac{\omega L}{a} \right) - 1} {\sin \left( \frac{\omega L}{a}\right)} \sin \left( \frac{\omega}{a} x \right) -1 \right) \cos ( \omega t)

concepts.name: Resonance of the forced string
concepts.statement: When sin(ωL/a) = 0, ω is a natural frequency nπa/L. For even n, cos(ωL/a) = 1 and B = 0 gives the bounded solution y_p = (F₀/ω²)(cos(ωx/a) − 1) cos(ωt), so no resonance happens; resonance occurs only when also cos(ωL/a) = −1, that is for odd n, where B blows up as ω approaches nπa/L. This is why a string begins to vibrate when an identical string is plucked close by, while a jet engine at the wrong frequency does not move it much.

concepts.name: Underground temperature model
concepts.statement: The temperature u(x, t) at depth x satisfies the heat equation u_t = ku_xx, k the diffusivity of the soil, with the surface temperature u(0, t) = T₀ + A₀ cos(ωt) known from weather records, t = 0 midsummer, ω with ωt = 2π at t = 1 year; taking T₀ = 0, the steady periodic solution, independent of the initial conditions, is sought in the form u = V(x) cos(ωt) + W(x) sin(ωt), equation (5.11).

forms.latex: u_t = k u_{xx}, \qquad u(0,t) = A_0 \cos ( \omega t)

concepts.name: Solving through a complex exponential
concepts.statement: To find the steady periodic solution, look for a complex-valued h(x, t) = X(x)e^(iωt) with h_t = kh_xx and h(0, t) = A₀e^(iωt), equation (5.12), and take u = Re h; substituting gives kX″ − iωX = 0, which is solved with complex exponents and Euler's formula.

forms.latex: h_t = k h_{xx}, \qquad h(0,t) = A_0 e^{i\omega t}

concepts.name: Underground temperature solution
concepts.statement: With α = ±(1 + i)√(ω/2k) and the growing exponential discarded as unbounded, h = A₀e^(−√(ω/2k) x) e^(i(ωt − √(ω/2k) x)), so u(x, t) = A₀e^(−√(ω/2k) x) cos(ωt − √(ω/2k) x): at depth x the phase is delayed by x√(ω/2k) and the amplitude is A₀e^(−√(ω/2k) x). In cgs units with k = 0.005 and ω ≈ 1.99 × 10⁻⁷, the seasons are reversed at about 700 cm, where a surface swing of ±15 °C is only ±0.66 °C, which is why a cellar keeps a nearly constant temperature.

forms.latex: u(x,t) = A_0 e^{-\sqrt{\frac{\omega}{2k}}\, x} \cos \left(\omega t - \sqrt{\frac{\omega}{2k}}\, x\right)
X(x) = A e^{-(1+i)\sqrt{\frac{\omega}{2k}} \, x} + B e^{(1+i)\sqrt{\frac{\omega}{2k}} \, x}
forms.ktex: \kX(x) = A e^{-(1+i)\sqrt{\frac{\komega}{2k}} \, x} + B e^{(1+i)\sqrt{\frac{\komega}{2k}} \, x}

concepts.name: Laplace transform
concepts.statement: The Laplace transform of a function f(t) is the function F(s) = ℒ{f(t)} = ∫ from 0 to ∞ of e^(−st) f(t) dt of the new variable s, defined for the s where the improper integral exists; only t ≥ 0 enters, a lower-case letter names the function in the time domain and the upper-case letter its transform.

concepts.name: Time domain and frequency domain
concepts.statement: The Laplace transform converts a differential equation in the time t into an algebraic equation in the new variable s, which is thought of as the frequency: the transform takes the equation from the time domain to the frequency domain, and the inverse transform brings the solution back.

concepts.name: Basic Laplace transforms
concepts.statement: Table 6.1 lists the transforms of the elementary functions, each computed from the definition: a constant C gives C/s, tⁿ gives n!/s^(n+1), e^(−at) gives 1/(s + a), sin ωt and cos ωt give ω/(s² + ω²) and s/(s² + ω²), sinh ωt and cosh ωt give ω/(s² − ω²) and s/(s² − ω²), and the shifted step u(t − a) gives e^(−as)/s, each for s large enough that the integral exists.

concepts.name: Unit step function
concepts.statement: The unit step function, or Heaviside function, is u(t) = 0 for t < 0 and u(t) = 1 for t ≥ 0; the shifted step u(t − a) is 0 for t < a and 1 for t ≥ a.

concepts.name: Linearity of the Laplace transform
concepts.statement: Theorem 6.1.1: if A, B and C are constants, then ℒ{Af(t) + Bg(t)} = Aℒ{f(t)} + Bℒ{g(t)}, and in particular ℒ{Cf(t)} = Cℒ{f(t)}, because the transform is defined by an integral; the transform of a product, however, is not the product of the transforms.

forms.latex: \mathcal{L} \bigl\{ A f(t) + B g(t) \bigr\} = A \mathcal{L} \bigl\{ f(t) \bigr\} + B \mathcal{L} \bigl\{ g(t) \bigr\}

concepts.name: Exponential order
concepts.statement: A function f(t) is of exponential order as t goes to infinity if |f(t)| ≤ Me^(ct) for some constants M and c and all sufficiently large t; the simplest check is that the limit of f(t)/e^(ct) as t → ∞ exists and is finite.

concepts.name: Existence of the Laplace transform
concepts.statement: Theorem 6.1.2: if f(t) is continuous on [0, ∞) and of exponential order for a constant c, then F(s) = ℒ{f(t)} is defined for all s > c; the improper integral exists by comparison with ∫ e^(−st) Me^(ct) dt = M/(s − c). The theorem holds for piecewise continuous functions as well.

concepts.name: Decay of the transform at infinity
concepts.statement: For a function of exponential order the Laplace transform decays at infinity: lim F(s) = 0 as s → ∞. So a rational function that is a transform must be proper, and a transformed problem whose Y does not decay has no solution.

concepts.name: Uniqueness of the Laplace transform
concepts.statement: Theorem 6.1.3: if f(t) and g(t) are continuous and of exponential order and F(s) = G(s) for all s > C, then f(t) = g(t) for all t ≥ 0. For piecewise continuous functions the transform does not see the values at the discontinuities, so f = g only outside them.

concepts.name: Inverse Laplace transform
concepts.statement: If F(s) = ℒ{f(t)} for some function f(t), the inverse Laplace transform of F(s) is ℒ⁻¹{F(s)} = f(t); it is well defined because the transform is unique, it is linear, and it is computed from the table rather than from its integral formula.

forms.latex: {\mathcal{L}}^{-1} \bigl\{ A F(s) + B G(s) \bigr\} = A {\mathcal{L}}^{-1} \bigl\{ F(s) \bigr\} + B {\mathcal{L}}^{-1} \bigl\{ G(s) \bigr\}

concepts.name: Method of partial fractions
concepts.statement: To invert a rational F(s), factor the denominator into linear and quadratic terms, write F as a sum of simpler fractions with unknown constants, put the sum over the common denominator and equate coefficients, then invert each piece with the table.

concepts.name: First shifting property
concepts.statement: Multiplying f(t) by e^(−at) shifts its transform: ℒ{e^(−at) f(t)} = F(s + a), where F(s) is the transform of f(t). It inverts a quadratic denominator after completing the square to (s + a)² + b.

concepts.name: Proper rational function
concepts.statement: A rational function F(s)/G(s), with F and G polynomials, is proper when the degree of F is smaller than that of G; the transform of an exponential-order function goes to zero as s → ∞, so it is a proper rational function and partial fractions apply without polynomial division.

concepts.name: Computing a Laplace transform
concepts.statement: Compute a transform from the definition as an improper integral (integrating by parts where needed), note the s for which the limit exists, and build the transforms of sums and constant multiples from the table by linearity.

concepts.name: Finding an inverse transform
concepts.statement: Write F(s) as a combination of table entries, by partial fractions where it is rational and by completing the square and the shifting property where a quadratic does not factor, then read the inverse of each piece from the table and add them by linearity.

concepts.name: Laplace transform of a derivative
concepts.statement: If g(t) is differentiable and of exponential order, then ℒ{g′(t)} = sG(s) − g(0), by integration by parts; repeating gives ℒ{g″} = s²G(s) − sg(0) − g′(0) and ℒ{g‴} = s³G(s) − s²g(0) − sg′(0) − g″(0) (Table 6.2). The transform turns differentiation into multiplication by s, and the rule also holds for continuous piecewise smooth functions.

concepts.name: Solving an ODE with the Laplace transform
concepts.statement: For a linear constant-coefficient equation in t: apply the transform to both sides, so x, x′, x″ become X(s), sX(s) − x(0), s²X(s) − sx(0) − x′(0), plug in the initial conditions, solve the algebraic equation for X(s), and take the inverse transform to find x(t). Not every function has a transform, and a non-constant-coefficient equation need not become algebraic.

concepts.name: Writing piecewise functions with the Heaviside function
concepts.statement: A function switched on at t = a is f(t)u(t − a), a step that is 1 on [a, b) and 0 elsewhere is u(t − a) − u(t − b), and a function defined piecewise is a sum of its pieces each multiplied by the difference of steps that cuts out its interval.

concepts.name: Second shifting property
concepts.statement: Equation (6.1): for a ≥ 0, ℒ{f(t − a) u(t − a)} = e^(−as) ℒ{f(t)}; delaying a function by a and switching it on at a multiplies its transform by e^(−as), which generalizes ℒ{u(t − a)} = e^(−as)/s and inverts a transform carrying the factor e^(−as).

concepts.name: Input and output of a system
concepts.statement: In an equation Lx = f(t), with L a linear constant-coefficient differential operator, f(t) is thought of as the input of the system and x(t) as its output; for a mass–spring system the input is the forcing function and the output is the behavior of the mass.

concepts.name: Transfer function
concepts.statement: With all initial conditions zero, transforming Lx = f(t) gives A(s)X(s) = F(s) for some A(s); the transfer function is the ratio H(s) = X(s)/F(s) = 1/A(s), so that X(s) = H(s)F(s): an algebraic dependence of the output on the input, which can be measured from one input–output pair and then gives the output for any input.

concepts.name: Laplace transform of an integral
concepts.statement: ℒ{∫ from 0 to t of f(τ) dτ} = F(s)/s, proved from the definition by integration by parts; read backwards, ℒ⁻¹{F(s)/s} = ∫ from 0 to t of f(τ) dτ, which computes an inverse transform by integrating a known one.

concepts.name: Integral equation
concepts.statement: An integral equation is an equation containing an integral of the unknown function; the Laplace transform turns the integral into division by s and the equation into an algebraic one.

concepts.name: Laplace transform of a periodic function
concepts.statement: If f(t) = f(t + P) for a period P, splitting the integral at P and shifting the tail gives F(s) = ∫₀ᴾ e^(−st) f(t) dt + e^(−Ps)F(s), so F(s) = (1/(1 − e^(−Ps))) ∫ from 0 to P of e^(−st) f(t) dt: one period's integral suffices.

concepts.name: Sawtooth of period 1
concepts.statement: A version of the sawtooth is f(t) = t for 0 ≤ t < 1 extended periodically by f(t) = f(t + 1), so f(t) = t − 1 on [1, 2), t − 2 on [2, 3), and so on; its period is 1 and its transform is 1/s² − e^(−s)/((1 − e^(−s))s).

concepts.name: Convolution
concepts.statement: The convolution of two functions f(t) and g(t) defined for t ≥ 0 is (f ∗ g)(t) = ∫ from 0 to t of f(τ) g(t − τ) dτ (equation (6.2)), another function of t; it is the different kind of product whose transform is the product of the transforms.

concepts.name: Properties of convolution
concepts.statement: Convolution behaves like a product: it is commutative, f ∗ g = g ∗ f; a constant comes out, (cf) ∗ g = f ∗ (cg) = c(f ∗ g); it distributes over addition, (f + g) ∗ h = f ∗ h + g ∗ h; and it is associative, (f ∗ g) ∗ h = f ∗ (g ∗ h).

forms.latex: ( f * g ) * h = f * ( g * h )

concepts.name: Convolution theorem
concepts.statement: Theorem 6.3.1: if f(t) and g(t) are of exponential order, so is (f ∗ g)(t), and ℒ{(f ∗ g)(t)} = ℒ{f(t)} ℒ{g(t)}: the transform of a convolution is the product of the transforms, F(s)G(s), and in reverse ℒ⁻¹{F(s)G(s)} = (f ∗ g)(t).

concepts.name: Inverting a product by convolution
concepts.statement: To invert a transform that is a product of two table entries, F(s)G(s), recognize f and g from the table and compute the convolution integral (f ∗ g)(t) instead of a partial fraction decomposition.

concepts.name: Solution as a convolution with the transfer function's inverse
concepts.statement: For a constant-coefficient equation Lx = f(t) with zero initial conditions, X(s) = H(s)F(s), so with h(t) = ℒ⁻¹{H(s)} the solution for any forcing f(t) is the definite integral x(t) = (f ∗ h)(t) = ∫ from 0 to t of f(τ) h(t − τ) dτ; for x″ + ω₀²x = f(t) it is x(t) = ∫ from 0 to t of f(τ) sin(ω₀(t − τ))/ω₀ dτ, which for f = cos ω₀t grows as t sin(ω₀t)/(2ω₀): resonance.

forms.latex: x(t) = {\mathcal{L}}^{-1}\bigl\{ F(s)H(s) \bigr\} = (f * h)(t) = \int_0^t f(\tau) h(t-\tau) \, d\tau

concepts.name: Volterra integral equation
concepts.statement: A Volterra integral equation is x(t) = f(t) + ∫ from 0 to t of g(t − τ) x(τ) dτ with f and g known, that is x = f + g ∗ x; it comes up in systems with memory effects, and transforming it gives X(s) = F(s) + G(s)X(s), so X(s) = F(s)/(1 − G(s)) and x is its inverse transform.

concepts.name: Impulse response
concepts.statement: The impulse response of a system Lx = f(t) is what the system does when the input is a short pulse: the solution h of Lx = δ(t) with zero initial conditions, which is the inverse transform of the transfer function, h(t) = ℒ⁻¹{H(s)}; knowing it tells how the system responds to any input.

concepts.name: Rectangular pulse
concepts.statement: A rectangular pulse is φ(t) = M for a ≤ t < b and 0 otherwise, that is φ(t) = M(u(t − a) − u(t − b)), with transform M(e^(−as) − e^(−bs))/s; with a = 0 and M = 1/b it has unit mass, ∫ φ dt = 1, and its transform (1 − e^(−bs))/(bs) tends to 1 as b → 0.

forms.latex: \varphi(t) = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } \; t < a , \\ M & \text{if } \; a \leq t < b , \\ 0 & \text{if } \; b \leq t . \end{cases}
forms.ktex: \kvarphi(t) = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } \; t < a , \\ M & \text{if } \; a \leq t < b , \\ 0 & \text{if } \; b \leq t . \end{cases}

concepts.name: Generalized function
concepts.statement: A generalized function is an object, like the Dirac delta, that is not exactly a function and does not really make sense unless it is integrated; a formula such as δ(t) + 1 is only meaningful underneath an integral.

concepts.name: Dirac delta function
concepts.statement: The Dirac delta function δ(t) is the generalized function with ∫ δ(t) f(t) dt = f(0) for every continuous f(t) over any interval containing 0: all its mass sits at the single point t = 0, so ∫ from c to d of δ(t) dt is 1 if c ≤ 0 ≤ d and 0 otherwise; shifted, ∫ δ(t − a) f(t) dt = f(a), and δ(a − t) is the same object as δ(t − a). Informally it is zero for t ≠ 0 and somehow infinite at t = 0.

concepts.name: The delta function as a limit of pulses
concepts.statement: A good way to think about δ(t) is as the limit of rectangular pulses of decreasing length b, each of integral 1: for φ(t) = (u(t) − u(t − b))/b and f continuous at 0, ∫ φ(t) f(t) dt = (1/b) ∫ from 0 to b of f(t) dt, which tends to f(0) as b → 0.

concepts.name: Convolution with the delta function
concepts.statement: The convolution of δ(t) with f(t) is f(t) again: (f ∗ δ)(t) = ∫ from 0 to t of f(τ) δ(t − τ) dτ = f(t), so δ is the identity for convolution.

concepts.name: Laplace transform of the delta function
concepts.statement: Since δ can be integrated, ℒ{δ(t − a)} = ∫ from 0 to ∞ of e^(−st) δ(t − a) dt = e^(−as), and in particular ℒ{δ(t)} = 1: the delta function is the object whose transform is 1, the limit of the unit-mass pulse's transform.

concepts.name: The delta function as the derivative of the Heaviside function
concepts.statement: Remark 6.4.1: multiplying ℒ{u(t − a)} = e^(−as)/s by s, as the transform of a derivative would, gives e^(−as) = ℒ{δ(t − a)}, and ∫ from 0 to t of δ(τ − a) dτ = u(t − a); so in a certain sense the derivative of u(t − a) is δ(t − a), somehow infinite at the jump, which lets one speak of derivatives of functions with jump discontinuities.

forms.condition: in the sense of generalized functions

concepts.name: Inverting an improper rational function
concepts.statement: When the numerator's degree is not lower than the denominator's, divide to split off a polynomial part and invert it with delta functions, ℒ⁻¹{1} = δ(t) and ℒ⁻¹{e^(−as)} = δ(t − a), then invert the proper remainder with the table; the result is a generalized function.

concepts.name: Finding the impulse response
concepts.statement: Put δ(t) in place of the input, transform the equation with zero initial conditions, so that the right-hand side becomes 1 and X(s) = H(s), and invert; the initial condition x′(0) = 0 is really x′(0−) = 0, since x has a corner at t = 0 whose jump in x′ produces the δ.

concepts.name: Derivative of a convolution
concepts.statement: For functions f(t) and h(t) that are zero for negative t, differentiating under the integral gives (f ∗ h)″(t) = (f ∗ h″)(t); so convolving the equation h″ + ω₀²h = δ with f shows that x = f ∗ h solves x″ + ω₀²x = f: the solution for an arbitrary input is the convolution with the impulse response.

forms.latex: (f * h)''(t) = \frac{d^2}{dt^2}\left[ \int_0^t f(\tau) h(t-\tau) \, d\tau \right] = \int_0^t f(\tau) h''(t-\tau) \, d\tau = (f * h'')(t)

concepts.name: Euler–Bernoulli equation
concepts.statement: The deflection y(x) of a beam satisfies EI y⁗ = F(x), where E (the elastic modulus) and I (the second moment of area) are constants and F(x) is the force applied per unit length at the position x.

concepts.name: Three-point beam bending
concepts.statement: A beam of length L rests on two simple supports at its ends and a force F pushes down at the single point x = a: the point load is a delta function, EI y⁗ = −Fδ(x − a), with y(0) = y″(0) = 0 and y(L) = y″(L) = 0 at the ends; the Laplace transform in the x variable, with the second shifting property, solves it.

concepts.name: Solving a PDE with the Laplace transform
concepts.statement: Given a PDE in x and t, transform everything in sight in the t variable, writing Y(x) = ℒ{y(x, t)} with s as a parameter: t-derivatives become multiplications by s, the side condition in t is used in the derivative rule, the PDE becomes an ODE in x whose initial condition is the transformed condition at x = 0; solve it, then invert, typically with the second shifting property. Laplace handles nonhomogeneous side conditions but is essentially only useful for constant-coefficient equations.

concepts.name: Transform of a partial derivative
concepts.statement: Transforming y(x, t) in t, the transform of a derivative with respect to x is the derivative of the transformed function, ℒ{y_x} = Y′(x), while a derivative in the transformed variable follows the rule of §6.2, ℒ{y_t} = sY(x) − y(x, 0).

concepts.name: Transport equation on a half line
concepts.statement: Example 6.5.1: for y_t = −αy_x on x > 0, t > 0 with y(0, t) = C and y(x, 0) = 0, the transformed problem sY = −αY′, Y(0) = C/s has Y(x) = (C/s) e^(−sx/α), so y(x, t) = C u(t − x/α): zero before the wavefront t = x/α arrives and C after; the equation moves the boundary condition to the right at speed α.

forms.latex: y(x,t) = {\mathcal L}^{-1} \left\{ \frac{C}{s} e^{-\frac{s}{\alpha} x} \right\} = C u\bigl(t-{x}/{\alpha}\bigr)

concepts.name: Wavefront
concepts.statement: The wavefront of the toxic substance is the line t = x/α of slope 1/α in the (x, t) plane, the edge between the region y = 0 ahead of it and y = C behind it, moving right at speed α; along it y jumps, and y_t and y_x are delta functions there.

concepts.name: Ill-posed problem
concepts.statement: A problem is ill-posed, in the sense used here, when it has no solution: for −y_t + y_x = 0 with y(0, t) = sin t and y(x, 0) = 0, the characteristics t = −x + C meet both axes, where the data disagree, and the transformed solution Y(x) = e^(sx)/(s² + 1) does not decay to zero as s → ∞, so it cannot be a Laplace transform.

concepts.name: Boundedness as a boundary condition
concepts.statement: On a half-infinite rod the solution is assumed bounded, and this boundedness condition stands in for a boundary condition at the infinite end: for fixed s > 0 the transformed Y(x) = Ae^(√s x) + Be^(−√s x) stays bounded only if A = 0. Boundedness also makes the transform in t exist.

concepts.name: Power series
concepts.statement: A power series is an expression Σ a_k(x − x₀)^k = a₀ + a₁(x − x₀) + a₂(x − x₀)² + ⋯, where a₀, a₁, a₂, … and x₀ are constants; many functions can be written in terms of one, and a solution of a differential equation can be sought as one.

concepts.name: Coefficients of a power series
concepts.statement: The constants a₀, a₁, a₂, …, a_k, … in a power series Σ a_k(x − x₀)^k are called its coefficients.

concepts.name: Center of a power series
concepts.statement: The constant x₀ in a power series Σ a_k(x − x₀)^k is called its center; at x = x₀ the series always converges, to a₀.

concepts.name: Partial sum
concepts.statement: The partial sum S_n(x) = Σ_{k=0}^n a_k(x − x₀)^k = a₀ + a₁(x − x₀) + ⋯ + a_n(x − x₀)ⁿ is the power series cut off after the nth power.

concepts.name: Convergent power series
concepts.statement: A power series converges at x if the limit of its partial sums S_n(x) as n → ∞ exists; it is a convergent power series if it converges at some x ≠ x₀, and then the series is that limit; it is divergent if it converges at no x ≠ x₀.

concepts.name: Absolute convergence
concepts.statement: A power series converges absolutely at x whenever Σ |a_k| |x − x₀|^k converges; if it converges absolutely at x then it converges at x, but the opposite implication is not true.

concepts.name: Radius of convergence
concepts.statement: The radius of convergence of a power series is the number ρ (ρ = ∞ allowed) such that the series converges absolutely on (x₀ − ρ, x₀ + ρ) and diverges when x < x₀ − ρ or x > x₀ + ρ; ρ = ∞ means the series converges for all x, and ρ = 0 is another way of saying the series is divergent.

concepts.name: Convergence of a power series
concepts.statement: For a power series Σ a_k(x − x₀)^k there exists a radius of convergence ρ: if the series converges absolutely at some x₁, it converges absolutely at every x no further from x₀ than x₁, since the smaller terms |a_k||x − x₀|^k are bounded by the summable |a_k||x₁ − x₀|^k; at the endpoints x₀ ± ρ the series may or may not converge.

concepts.name: Ratio test
concepts.statement: For a series Σ c_k, if the limit L = lim |c_{k+1}/c_k| exists, then the series converges absolutely if L < 1 and diverges if L > 1.

concepts.name: Root test
concepts.statement: For a series Σ c_k, if the limit L = lim ᵏ√|c_k| exists, then the series converges absolutely if L < 1 and diverges if L > 1.

concepts.name: Ratio and root tests for power series
concepts.statement: For a power series Σ a_k(x − x₀)^k such that A = lim |a_{k+1}/a_k| or A = lim ᵏ√|a_k| exists: if A = 0 the radius of convergence is ∞, otherwise it is 1/A, and if either limit diverges to ∞ the series is divergent. The tests say nothing about the endpoints, and where the limit for A does not exist the test is applied to the series itself to find L.

forms.condition: A > 0; the radius is ∞ when A = 0

concepts.name: Analytic function
concepts.statement: Functions represented by power series are called analytic: an analytic function f(x) equals its Taylor series for x near a given point x₀. Not all functions are analytic, but the functions seen in calculus likely all are.

concepts.name: Taylor series
concepts.statement: The Taylor series of f around x₀ is the power series computed from f, Σ f^{(k)}(x₀)/k! (x − x₀)^k = f(x₀) + f′(x₀)(x − x₀) + f″(x₀)/2 (x − x₀)² + ⋯, where f^{(k)}(x₀) is the kth derivative of f at x₀; the approximation is very good for x near x₀ and gets worse further away, so more terms are needed far from x₀.

concepts.name: Series of the exponential and the sine
concepts.statement: The exponential and the sine are analytic with series that converge at every x: eˣ = Σ x^k/k!, with a_k = 1/k! and 0! = 1, and sin x = Σ (−1)ⁿ x^{2n+1}/(2n + 1)! around x₀ = 0.

concepts.name: Term-by-term differentiation
concepts.statement: A convergent power series can be differentiated term by term: for x within the radius of convergence, d/dx Σ a_k(x − x₀)^k = Σ_{k≥1} k a_k(x − x₀)^{k−1} = a₁ + 2a₂(x − x₀) + 3a₃(x − x₀)² + ⋯, the k = 0 term disappearing as it was constant; the differentiated series has the same radius of convergence as the original.

forms.latex: \frac{d}{dx} \left[\sum_{k=0}^\infty a_k {(x-x_0)}^k\right] = \sum_{k=1}^\infty k a_k {(x-x_0)}^{k-1} = a_1 + 2 a_2 (x-x_0) + 3 a_3 {(x-x_0)}^{2} + \cdots

concepts.name: Reindexing a series
concepts.statement: To reindex a series, replace k by k + 1 (or another shift) throughout, so that the series starts at k = 0 again; the series does not change, only how it is written, as when Σ_{k≥1} x^{k−1}/(k − 1)! becomes Σ_{k≥0} x^k/k!.

concepts.name: Sum and constant multiple of power series
concepts.statement: Convergent power series are added term by term, (Σ a_k(x − x₀)^k) + (Σ b_k(x − x₀)^k) = Σ (a_k + b_k)(x − x₀)^k, and multiplied by a constant term by term, α Σ a_k(x − x₀)^k = Σ αa_k(x − x₀)^k; the radius of convergence of the sum is at least the minimum of the two radii.

concepts.name: Product of power series
concepts.statement: Two convergent power series multiply to a power series, (Σ a_k(x − x₀)^k)(Σ b_k(x − x₀)^k) = Σ c_k(x − x₀)^k with c_k = a₀b_k + a₁b_{k−1} + ⋯ + a_kb₀; the radius of convergence of the product is at least the minimum of the two radii.

forms.latex: c_k = a_0b_k + a_1 b_{k-1} + \cdots + a_k b_0

concepts.name: Polynomials as finite power series
concepts.statement: A polynomial is a finite power series, one whose coefficients a_k are zero for all large enough k; it expands as a power series about any point x₀ by writing it as a polynomial in (x − x₀), either by expanding a₀ + a₁(x − x₀) + ⋯ and solving for the coefficients or by differentiating at x₀ and using the Taylor series formula, as 2x² − 3x + 4 = 3 + (x − 1) + 2(x − 1)².

concepts.name: Geometric series
concepts.statement: The geometric series is 1/(1 − x) = Σ x^k = 1 + x + x² + ⋯ for −1 < x < 1; its radius of convergence is 1 by the ratio test, and it diverges for x ≤ −1 and x ≥ 1 even though 1/(1 − x) is defined for all x ≠ 1: a series for a function only defines the function on an interval.

concepts.name: Expanding a rational function
concepts.statement: A rational function, a ratio of polynomials, expands around any x₀ where its denominator is not zero by the geometric series together with the rules for adding and multiplying power series, or by partial fractions when it is more complicated, instead of the Taylor series formula; the radius of convergence is then checked with the ratio test, as for x/(1 + 2x + x²) = Σ (−1)^{k+1} k x^k with radius 1.

concepts.name: Ordinary point
concepts.statement: For the linear second-order homogeneous equation P(x)y″ + Q(x)y′ + R(x)y = 0 with polynomial P, Q, R, the point x₀ is an ordinary point if P(x₀) ≠ 0, that is, Q(x)/P(x) and R(x)/P(x) are defined for x near x₀; a power series solution y = Σ a_k(x − x₀)^k is then sought in some interval around x₀.

forms.latex: P(x) y'' + Q(x) y' + R(x) y = 0

concepts.name: Singular point
concepts.statement: If P(x₀) = 0, then x₀ is a singular point of P(x)y″ + Q(x)y′ + R(x)y = 0; handling singular points is harder than handling ordinary points, and at one the power series method may find only the trivial solution y = 0.

concepts.name: Solving an equation by power series
